articles.title: What are AI chips, and what’s so special about Nvidia’s?
articles.author: Jeffrey Young, Principal Research Scientist, Partnership for an Advanced Computing Environment, Georgia Institute of Technology
paras: The commotion around Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s ouster and reinstatement, the central role of Nvidia in the U.S.-China AI competition, and the U.S. economy’s reliance on the AI boom might leave you asking: What’s so special about Nvidia’s chips?
The answer comes down to graphics processing units, or GPUs, and how far they’ve come from their humble beginnings as sidekicks to computers’ main chips: central processing units, or CPUs.
GPUs now power the most visible advances in generative artificial intelligence, but they began as modestly priced add-on cards for video games and video rendering.

As a researcher of high-performance computing and computer processors, I see three factors that explain how GPUs have become so important to the modern economy and how Nvidia became their dominant supplier: software that made GPUs useful beyond graphics, a research breakthrough that showed what they could do for AI, and a global commercial and political race to build ever-larger AI models.

The CPU is built to handle a wide variety of complicated tasks quickly, a few at a time. In contrast, a GPU typically operates on simpler mathematical tasks, such as multiplying two sets of numbers, but it can perform many of these simpler operations in parallel.

A GPU’s design turns out to be ideal for AI. Training a neural network, the kind of AI model behind today’s chatbots and image generators, comes down mostly to multiplying enormous grids of numbers, over and over. Today’s top AI GPUs can perform more than a quadrillion, or thousand trillion, of these operations every second.
From pretty pictures to AI data centers

Early GPUs could only draw graphics. Programmers controlled them with small programs called shaders, which calculate things such as the color of each pixel and which can be repeated across millions of pixels in parallel. Nvidia dominated the market for graphics chips in the late 1990s and 2000s.

In the early 2000s, Stanford University researchers built software tools that let programmers use this hardware for other kinds of calculations. That work provided the basis for Nvidia’s Compute Unified Device Architecture, or CUDA, which was released in 2007. CUDA allowed scientists and engineers to run scientific and more general purpose programs using the GPU’s parallel execution model.

The second major shift occurred when AlexNet, a neural network model developed and trained on GPUs, won the 2012 ImageNet challenge, an annual competition to see which software could most accurately identify objects in a set of photographs. AlexNet was trained on two Nvidia GPUs, and it made far fewer mistakes than any competitor. The result showed that GPUs made it practical to train neural networks big enough to beat the older techniques, and AI researchers quickly adopted them for their work.

Because Nvidia had spent years building CUDA and the software around it, it was positioned to benefit more than anyone. Competitors, including AMD, which also makes GPUs, and Google, which designs its own AI chips, called tensor processing units, have since built strong alternatives.

Nvidia and other chipmakers then began redesigning GPUs for AI with specific features. These include adding hardware specialized for the matrix multiplication math that neural networks rely on, using reduced precision numbers to improve the speed of neural network training and adding larger amounts of fast memory to keep these chips supplied with data for AI workloads.

In 2017, Google researchers introduced the transformer, a neural network design originally built to translate between languages. Transformers turned out to perform remarkably well in terms of accuracy as the model and dataset size grew, and this design became the foundation of today’s chatbots and many other generative AI systems.

The growth of these new transformer models has also led to the current boom of generative AI companies, including U.S.-based companies OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, Google and xAI, as well as Chinese companies such as DeepSeek, Alibaba and Baidu. Each of these companies is actively focused on building large data centers composed of high-end GPUs to train next-generation foundation models.

These foundation models, exemplified by Google’s Gemini, Anthropic’s Claude Fable and OpenAI’s GPT Astra, are very large neural networks that can reason, write software code and analyze information in response to plain language instructions. The companies working on foundation model training are betting that the best models will automate much of the world’s information work and generate enormous economic returns.

Nvidia trains some AI models of its own, but most of its profit comes from selling the chips and software that other companies use to build theirs. This AI boom has led to record profits for Nvidia, but it has also drawn attention from the U.S. government, which has debated how far to restrict sales of advanced chips to China. The Trump administration tightened its export controls for advanced GPUs in the immediate aftermath of the scandal involving Huang’s relationship with an alleged Chinese spy.

Demand for AI chips looks likely to keep growing as the leading AI companies compete to build more capable models, but the boom faces real limits. AI data centers require enormous amounts of electricity, raising questions about the power costs and environmental impacts to local communities.

The most advanced AI chips, including Nvidia’s, are fabricated largely by one company, Taiwanese chip giant Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., known as TSMC. Demand for AI hardware has also strained supplies of memory chips, creating shortages that reach gaming graphics cards and smartphones.

Nvidia also faces direct competition from AMD, cloud companies designing their own chips, and startups, all promising to run AI more cheaply and with less power. Whether Nvidia’s software and hardware advantages can hold off these challengers is one of the biggest open questions in the industry.

articles.title: From solving to ‘digesting’: How mathematicians can adapt to the dramatic changes AI has brought to their field
articles.author: David Manderscheid, Professor of Mathematics, University of Tennessee
paras: Mathematics is having an existential crisis.

On Nov. 20, 2026, a mathematician at the AI company Anthropic claimed that while working with the model Claude, he had solved the generalized Riemann hypothesis, the most famous problem in mathematics. This problem has stood unsolved for 167 years, and solving it could easily warrant a Fields Medal – considered equivalent to a Nobel Prize, but for mathematics. In its current state, however, the solution is roughly 250,000 pages long, so it will take a while before human mathematicians can be satisfied that it is correct.

This proof emerged a month after OpenAI released 722 mathematics research papers that contained results generated by an internal AI model. While they have already retracted some of the papers due to mistakes, others, assuming they are correct, would also be impressive enough to earn a Fields Medal.

If AI can generate papers that would take a human mathematician years to research and write, does that mean mathematics is dead? Many headlines have been asking this question – and some school-age children may be rejoicing.

But it’s not that simple. I’ve been a mathematician for 45 years, and my work has taught me that mathematics is not just about solving problems or proving theorems. It is about understanding why the solutions and proofs work and then extending that mathematics to new contexts.

Fueling this existential crisis is the fact that over the past century, mathematicians have come to attach greater prestige to the solution and the proof than the understanding. Now that an AI can come up with a solution and a proof, the underlying understanding could vanish. Mathematicians are being forced to rethink what they value.
Why should nonmathematicians care?
If you’re not a mathematician, this crisis might seem inconsequential. But math isn’t all abstract problems. It’s used to design and optimize technology that’s essential to modern society.

One example is MRI, or magnetic resonance imaging. MRI is a very useful tool in medical diagnosis. X-rays see only your bones, but MRI machines allow a physician to see the soft tissue inside a person in a noninvasive manner.

MRI scans used to require a patient to lie still inside a metal tube for up to half an hour or more while a loud machine made images by scanning back and forth. At the end, it combined the images. This process was difficult for many adults and virtually impossible for children without sedation.

Modern MRI machines require many fewer scans in a shorter period, and they get better resolution. Now, more patients find the procedure no big deal. The key to this vast improvement was the mathematics of compressed sensing, a relatively recent invention.

Compressed sensing allows the machine to construct an image from fewer scans. At first, doing so didn’t seem possible. But in the mid 2000s, a mathematician, statisticians and an electrical engineer figured out how to use the fact that many of the scans are very similar to develop the mathematics that made compressed sensing possible.

They showed that images can be reconstructed from far fewer samples than previously thought necessary. This solution required a deep understanding of many different areas of mathematics, and even the development of new mathematics. Moreover, it involved asking the right questions – something I believe current AI models would not have known how to do.

Today’s iterations of AI may have been able to speed up the invention of compressed sensing, with humans in the loop. But coming up with the mathematics behind compressed sensing most likely would have been beyond the current capabilities of AI by itself.

AI-led research still requires the involvement of human mathematicians. But mathematicians are now asking each other what they have to change about their approach and the field’s norms. Many problems that would have been given to Ph.D. students to solve for their dissertation can now be done by AI.

But most of Open AI’s 722 mathematics research papers are not understandable to a human mathematician, and this is certainly the case for the claimed proof of the generalized Riemann hypothesis. Even the outputs from these papers that have gone through the proof-checking software Lean, which can verify a proof, are often incomprehensible to a human. AI’s current mathematical writing ability is quite primitive.

In other words, the mathematics will be known to be true by the mathematicians, but they won’t have a clue in most cases as to why it is true. And if there is no understanding as to why, then the mathematics loses its value. If you don’t know why it works, then you can’t apply the math.

As Terrence Tao, the mathematician who solved the MRI problem, has said, mathematicians will now have to place value on the digestion of the proofs. By digestion he means absorbing, simplifying and contextualizing the proof.

Once digested, researchers gain understanding, and then the ability to apply the results in new realms. Many mathematicians are now arguing that Ph.D. programs should change their emphasis from solving a problem to solving, digesting and then showing understanding by explaining the solution to other mathematicians and colleagues in other scientific fields.

Mathematicians will also have to change how they teach their classes. AI can now easily solve any standard math homework problem. To get around this, instructors might try to design their classes around understanding, rather than reaching solutions. They might accomplish this shift using oral exams or class presentations.

Many mathematicians – me included – view this shift in the field as an opportunity to emphasize understanding. The invention of the calculator freed students from computation. AI may do the same at another level.

AI is not just changing mathematics. It will affect other disciplines, too. It is already speeding up the development of new materials and chemicals. In these fields, human scientists will still want to verify that the model yields what they desire.

Four years ago, ChatGPT was incapable of basic arithmetic. These models have progressed very quickly, so it’s hard to say where mathematics will be in the future. But regardless, learning math teaches students important problem-solving and critical-thinking skills that AI cannot, at least at this point in time, entirely replace.
David Manderscheid is on the National Academy of Sciences Board of Mathematical Sciences and Analytics and the Board of Trustees of the Institute for Pure and Applied Mathematics.

articles.title: What is resilience? It may be less about bouncing back than we think
articles.author: Chao Fang, Lecturer in Sociology, Deputy Director of the Centre for Ageing and the Life Course, University of Liverpool
paras: Resilience can sound empowering. Yet it can also become a responsibility, a socially imposed burden that people are expected to demonstrate when they are ill, ageing or struggling.

We are often told to be resilient. Mental health guidance, the media and even governments encourage us to become more resilient, as though resilience is something that we can build up and draw upon when life becomes difficult.

But resilience is not a superpower possessed by a fortunate few, nor simply a predetermined psychological resource that people carry with them. Rather, it is constituted through the relationships, routines, past experiences and opportunities to adapt. We don’t do it alone.

This matters because social conditions can make adapting to adversity easier or harder. Secure work, supportive relationships, accessible healthcare and financial resources can make it easier to to cope. Insecurity, isolation, poor health and limited alternatives can constrain our capacity to adapt.

In our research we followed people aged over 50 living with long COVID through three interviews conducted over 18 months. Their accounts take us beyond the popular idea of resilience as “bouncing back”. Instead, they show resilience being continually negotiated through relationships, external resources and wider social circumstances, as people navigate what has changed, what remains possible and what future they can imagine.

Caroline, 52, worked as a care worker on a zero-hours contract while living with persistent fatigue and brain fog, with little room to slow down or stop. She said, without work, “I don’t get any money”. She described taking only “a couple of minutes’ breather between each job” before carrying on.
She also felt pressure to appear as though she was coping: “I have to pretend that I’m alright, and then of course when I come home, it’s when I’m not.”

From a distance, this might look like resilience. But Caroline’s determination to keep going was shaped by financial insecurity and limited alternatives. Her capacity to adapt cannot be separated from the conditions in which she was trying to do so.
When resilience becomes an individual responsibility, people may feel pressured to pretend they are coping rather than seek support. This expectation to be resilient can itself become another burden.

Long Covid made these pressures particularly visible for the participants in our study. Its fluctuating symptoms could make it difficult to know whether changing capacities reflected illness, ageing or both. For people in their 50s and 60s, this could create a feeling of ageing “too soon”, while older participants sometimes faced assumptions that declining health was part of getting older.

Elizabeth, in her early 50s, described feeling trapped in a body that seemed much older than her age. Although others saw her as “back to normal”, she continued to struggle. There was, she said, “a bit of a gap between how people perceive you and how you’re feeling yourself”. Eventually, she described having to “fake it to make it”.

Her experience shows that resilience is not only shaped by material circumstances, but also by how other people understand us. Expectations about what someone of a particular age should be able to do can influence how they understand their own limitations.
Caroline and Elizabeth’s experiences remind us that when resilience becomes an individuality responsibility, it can lose its positive meaning.
These experiences challenge the idea that resilience is something innate we either have or lack. Instead, it is continually negotiated.

One way to imagine this is that resilience is less like armour and more like an immune system. Armour protects us by keeping adversity out. An immune system responds to what it encounters, interacting with its surrounding environment and continually adjusting. Similarly, social conditions make resilience possible.
Kenneth, 61, was depressed in his first interview with us after losing work and hobbies. By the second, he had started a full-time job with a local council.

“Getting out and meeting people is great and feeling useful is great,” he said, linking his recovery closely to work and community participation: “If I was to draw a graph [of recovery and work], they would be very closely correlated.”

Arnold, 73, told us he experienced brain fog, vision loss and cardiac symptoms from long Covid, alongside the effects of a stroke more than ten years earlier. This left him reliant on his wife for many things. He described how he and his wife coped together: “we live for today”.
Yet when his wife died during the study, this shared way of coping was disrupted. His world became much smaller. His focus increasingly centred on simply getting through each day.
Kenneth and Arnold’s experiences show how resilience is not a fixed state, but something that can be strengthened, disrupted and reworked over time.

This matters beyond long Covid and ageing. Life brings uncertainties that cannot always be overcome; ill health, bereavement, changing relationships and shifting ideas about the future. Resilience may involve renegotiating who we are and what a good life might look like as these changes unfold.
It can mean adapting. It can mean accepting help. It can mean relinquishing an earlier version of ourselves.
Telling people to “be resilient” can obscure the conditions that make coping possible, including secure work, supportive relationships, accessible healthcare and financial resources.
Our research shows that resilience is an ongoing, often fragile way of living with uncertainty.

articles.title: What was the first animal that ever lived on Earth?
articles.author: Matthew W. Brown, Dr. Donald L. Hall Professor of Biology, Mississippi State University
paras: Curious Kids is a series for children of all ages. If you have a question you’d like an expert to answer, send it to CuriousKidsUS@theconversation.com.
What was the first animal on Earth? – Keira, age 10, Eugene, Oregon, and Julian, age 7, South Bend, Indiana
Imagine climbing into a time machine and setting the dial for when the very first animal was alive. You would need to travel really, really far back in time.

You would blow past the dinosaurs, which showed up about 230 million years ago. Keep going and you’d pass coil-shelled ammonites that swam in the oceans starting 450 million years ago, and then trilobites, armored animals that scuttled across the seafloor more than 520 million years ago. Further still, around 558 million years ago, you would meet Dickinsonia, a tiny, flat, ribbed oval only a few millimeters thick that looks more like a squashed pancake than any animal you know.
And even Dickinsonia was almost certainly not the first animal.
We are biologists who study single-celled life called protists. How complex life such as human beings showed up in the first place is one of the major questions in our field.
Honestly, nobody can name the first animal, but there are many clues about what it was probably like.
What makes an animal an animal?
If we asked you what an animal is, you might say something that moves, eats and reproduces. The trouble is that plenty of nonanimals do all three.
For instance, single-celled amoebae crawl, hunt and swallow their prey whole – and they are not animals at all!

Biologists define an animal as an organism made of many cells that stick together, communicate and divide up the work of growing, eating and moving. Different types of cells specialize to do different jobs, and they all work together as one organism. And when animals eat, they take in outside material instead of making their own food from sunlight the way plants do.
Notice what is not on that list: Legs. Eyes. A brain. A mouth. That matters for what comes next.

SpongeBob SquarePants is a cartoon version of a real animal, the sea sponge. Real sponges do not wear square pants; they don’t even move around. They sit anchored to the seafloor, pumping seawater through thousands of tiny holes and straining out bacteria to eat. They have no brain, no heart and no muscles.

But sponges are still animals, and scientists often think of them as the simplest ones. Part of what makes them so interesting is a type of cell they have called choanocytes. Each choanocyte has a whiplike tail ringed by tiny fingerlike projections that trap food.

Choanocytes look almost exactly like choanoflagellates, free-living, single-celled organisms that are the closest living relatives of animals. Watching a colony of choanoflagellates feed together is about as close as you can get to seeing the doorway between single-celled life and animal life.
Or were comb jellies first?

Imagine climbing down the animal tree of life going backward in time. You can start with animals alive today, which would be the leaves of the tree. Branches join where you encounter ancestors shared by different groups. Follow them far enough, and they all meet at a common ancestor of living animals. Scientists disagree about which groups belong on each side of that deepest branching point.

Some studies put sponges alone on one side of that fork, with every other living animal group, including us, on the other. Other studies put comb jellies in that position. In that case, these shimmering, jellylike ocean swimmers would occupy one side, while sponges and all other animals would occupy the other. This is what scientists mean when they describe either group as having “branched off first.”

It is important to remember that “branched off first” does not mean “unchanged.” Sponges, comb jellies and humans have all been evolving for the same amount of time, since our shared ancestor lived. Each lineage has followed its own evolutionary path, which over time has led to the great diversity of animals we see today, such as worms, insects, crabs and primates. Today’s sponges and comb jellies may therefore look very different from that common ancestor, making it difficult to picture what the first animal looked like.
What kinds of evidence tell the story?
Comparative biology can take us only so far.

Fossils are another source of information, but they show just a very narrow window into the past. Fossilization turns living material into stone, a process that works far better on hard parts such as shells, teeth and bones than on soft, squishy bodies. Because early animals were probably soft and small, they were likely easily erased from the record.

Also, fossilization works better in some kinds of environments than others. For example, muddy lake bottoms can bury dead organisms, protecting their remains from rapid decay so they have time to fossilize; any remains on wave-battered shores may wash away before they can fossilize.

Another line of evidence now available to scientists is genetic information. Genes, encoded in DNA strands inside every living organism, provide an instruction manual for how to build that creature. Cells copy that DNA and pass it on – a process that’s been going on for billions of years, generation after generation.

This genetic information accumulates slight changes over time, which scientists call mutations. It is the very existence of mutations that allows evolution – how life changes over time – to happen. This process is what generated the diversity of life you see today.

By studying the structure and architecture of DNA, as well as how it gets passed along, scientists can mathematically assemble family trees that extend very deep into the past. These family trees can help scientists make surprisingly good guesses about when and where an animal first arose. A creature’s genes hint at what it could possibly do.
Animals were assembled, not invented
Biologist Iñaki Ruiz-Trillo and his colleagues use a smartphone analogy that we find particularly useful when talking about the origin of animals.
A smartphone was not invented from scratch. Cameras, telephones, computers and the internet were all invented separately first. The innovation was combining them into a single piece of equipment.

Animals may have evolved in a similar way. Genes for sticking cells together, for sending signals between cells, for sensing the environment and for switching other genes on and off were already present in our single-celled relatives. Becoming an animal meant assembling that tool kit into one cooperating body.

The first animal was probably something very small, soft and unremarkable in an ancient ocean. It probably evolved over 650 million years ago. It certainly had different kinds of cells that were stuck together, doing specialized jobs.

Scientists may never be able to pinpoint the first animal, and we have a hard time trying to imagine it. But we do know that many of the cellular and molecular tools that helped early animal cells work together are still at work in your body today.

Hello, curious kids! Do you have a question you’d like an expert to answer? Ask an adult to send your question to CuriousKidsUS@theconversation.com. Please tell us your name, age and the city where you live.
And since curiosity has no age limit – adults, let us know what you’re wondering, too. We won’t be able to answer every question, but we will do our best.

articles.title: A fungus that can survive in Chernobyl could help create materials that trap and break down nerve agents and pesticides
articles.author: Sofia Aman, PhD Researcher in Materials Science and Engineering, Northwestern University
paras: Deep inside the Chernobyl exclusion zone, where radiation levels have remained unsafe for people for the past 40 years, black molds climb the walls of the damaged former nuclear plant in Ukraine. They’re entirely undeterred by the radiation – in fact, some fungi even grow toward it.

The same type of species, Cladosporium sphaerospermum, has grown on the International Space Station, about 250 miles (400 kilometers) above the surface of the Earth, in an experiment to test its resistance to radiation. Scientists found that it appeared to block a small amount of incoming radiation, and part of why comes down to a pigment called melanin.

I used to think of melanin the way most people do – as a pigment that gives skin, hair and eyes their color. That changed early in my Ph.D. research when I read a 2019 study from the materials science lab I was joining that described how to make a fungal form of melanin in the lab. I was surprised by where this pigment shows up in nature, including in fungi growing at Chernobyl.

Melanin comprises a family of pigments. The melanin in human skin, called eumelanin, is built from nitrogen-containing building blocks. The melanin in many fungi, called allomelanin, is built from a different, nitrogen-free building block. That difference in structure gives it some unusual properties.

Scientists think allomelanin is a large part of why these fungi can live in such places. Over the course of my doctoral research, I learned that melanin does much more than add color. It holds onto metals, absorbs ultraviolet light, converts light into heat and helps produce the colors of some bird feathers.

Allomelanin has another remarkable property. My colleagues showed in 2021 that lab-made allomelanin is full of built-in pores, each less than a billionth of a meter wide. Chemists call these pores “intrinsic pores” because they are part of the material’s natural structure, rather than etched in later. To our knowledge, it is the only type of melanin with built-in porosity.

These nanometer-wide pores let the pigment act like a sponge for small molecules, including toxic ones, a feature we confirmed holds true whether the allomelanin comes directly from natural fungi or whether it is synthesized in our lab.
In a recent study published in the peer-reviewed scientific journal ACS Nano, my colleagues and I asked whether this material could do more than trap toxic chemicals. Could it also break them down?
Chemistry behind nerve agents and pesticides

Nerve agents such as sarin and VX belong to a group of chemicals called organophosphorus compounds. They block an enzyme the body uses to switch off nerve signals. Without that enzyme, nerves keep firing continuously, and a large enough exposure can turn lethal within minutes.

Chemical weapons are banned under international law, but they remain a persistent security concern. In May 2026, inspectors from the Organization for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons reported discovering dozens of previously undeclared chemical weapons in Syria left over from the Assad government.

Many pesticides used on agricultural crops rely on this exact same underlying chemistry. A 2026 analysis estimated that accidental pesticide poisonings number in the hundreds of millions each year, resulting in roughly 11,000 deaths annually around the world. Farmworkers operating with minimal protective gear face the greatest ongoing risk.

Today’s protective suits mostly rely on materials like activated carbon, which trap the chemicals but don’t break them down. Soldiers and farmworkers could benefit from protective gear that does more than block these toxic chemicals. Researchers, including my colleagues, are working on materials that could neutralize them as well.
Adding a catalyst: Turning a sponge into scissors

Allomelanin on its own holds on to these organophosphorus molecules but leaves them chemically intact. A contaminated glove or mask that has merely trapped these toxins would remain hazardous to handle.

To improve our sponge, my colleagues and I made allomelanin in the form of tiny spheres, each hundreds of times narrower than a human hair. We then added tiny clusters made of a metal called zirconium. Each cluster consists of six zirconium atoms anchored by oxygen – it looks like a tiny cage of zirconium held together by oxygen.

Similar zirconium clusters form the active core of metal-organic frameworks, which are among the most studied materials for degrading chemical weapons. These clusters act like molecular scissors: When exposed to ambient moisture, they snip the chemical bonds holding organophosphates together, splitting them into less harmful pieces.
We tested different ways to attach these metal clusters to our synthetic allomelanin particles, ensuring the molecular scissors sat right where incoming toxins would land.

For safety, we tested the particles with a chemical stand-in widely used in research laboratories. It mimics nerve agents but carries far less toxicity. Our best-performing versions broke down half of the target chemical in less than 10 minutes, using only a tiny amount of zirconium. The particles kept working over several rounds of use, with very little metal leaking out.

Allomelanin’s built-in pores turned out to be essential. When we added the same zirconium clusters to other melanin-like materials without pores, they barely facilitated the breakdown. Adding too much zirconium also slowed the reaction, likely because more clusters clogged up the pores that water and toxic molecules needed to travel through. The best results came from balancing the amount of metal with open pore space.
Using sunlight to power the cleanup
This reaction usually needs alkaline conditions, which have a high pH and are the opposite of acidic – for example, baking soda dissolved in water is alkaline.

Water alone breaks down the trapped molecules far too slowly, over weeks or months. Alkaline conditions supply hydroxide, a negatively charged relative of water that is drawn to the molecule’s most dangerous bond and helps the zirconium snap it in minutes. In the lab, that means we add a liquid chemical to make the conditions alkaline, but doing so isn’t practical for a soldier’s jacket or a farmworker’s mask. Instead, we attached alkaline chemical groups directly to the particle surfaces.

We then took advantage of another property of melanin: It absorbs light and turns it into heat. Under a bright lamp for five minutes, the particles broke down about 10 times more of the stand-in chemical than they did in the dark. Simply heating the samples in the dark had a much smaller effect, which suggests light does more than warm the particles.

Our work has important limits. We tested a chemical surrogate in laboratory vials rather than using live nerve agents or agricultural pesticides floating in the air. We also have not yet woven these particles into commercial textiles. Our immediate next steps are to evaluate the material against the specific pesticides farmworkers encounter daily and to refine the particle coating process.

Getting the material into fabrics may be more straightforward than it sounds. Synthetic melanin naturally adheres to textile fibers without needing chemical glues, and our research group has previously demonstrated that synthetic melanins could act as sustainable fabric dyes.

In the future, we hope this work can help develop lightweight gloves, masks and uniforms that continuously destroy toxic chemicals on contact as people work in the sun. Zirconium is a common and relatively inexpensive metal, and each particle uses only a small amount, though we haven’t evaluated what the cost of making these materials at a larger scale could be.
More broadly, this study highlights the untapped potential of natural materials. Fungi spent millions of years evolving pigments to endure some of the harshest environments on Earth.
I started my Ph.D. thinking of melanin simply as a biological colorant. I now see it as a versatile, multifunctional material whose full capabilities we are only beginning to unlock.

articles.title: Technology for ‘printing’ steel could help extend the life of ageing bridges and buildings
articles.author: Barbara Rossi, Associate Professor and Tutorial Fellow in Engineering Science (Structures & Mechanics), University of Oxford
paras: The UK has an enormous amount of steel in service across critical infrastructure. Yet every day, millions of people cross bridges without giving much thought to the structures beneath their feet.

Many of these structures are far older than we might imagine, and they survive under demands their original designers could hardly have anticipated. But ageing infrastructure cannot be taken for granted.

As a recent report from the Royal Academy of Engineering warned: “The need to act is urgent. Many of our ageing assets are approaching a critical state where they risk compromising the reliability of the services they provide.”
Addressing this requires extending the life of steel structures in their primary functions. This may involve using additional steel for repairs or replacing part of the structure.

Steel production – including low carbon methods – and steel recycling are both carbon-intensive, so there’s an impact on the climate. The question is therefore not whether we need to intervene, but how best to intervene.

In the UK, around 300 million tonnes (Mt) of iron and steel are embedded in buildings and what’s known as mobility infrastructure: the systems that support the safe and efficient movement of people. If life extension allowed just 1% of this stock to remain in service instead of being replaced, 3 Mt of steel production could be avoided.

Even when using greener methods of steel manufacturing, such as scrap electric arc furnace production, this would correspond to approximately 2.1 million tonnes of carbon dioxide-equivalent (MtCO₂e) and 8.2 terawatt-hours (TWh) of steelmaking energy. In a future where low-carbon steel production competes for constrained supplies of clean electricity, hydrogen and carbon dioxide from carbon capture, the tonne of steel that uses fewest resources is the tonne we do not produce.

Yet repairing structures often requires disproportionately extensive, costly and disruptive interventions – and comes with its own carbon cost. What if instead we could encourage purpose driven innovations that extend the life of ageing structural steel for generations to come?

Imagine an old steel bridge with a section weakened by fatigue cracks. Traditionally, engineers would reinforce the damaged region by attaching additional steel plates or replacing part of the structure.

Today, additive manufacturing allows us to restore deteriorated steel precisely where it is needed, without replacing entire structural components. It is a process where three-dimensional objects are built up layer by layer from a digital model.

The German company Siemens and US-based Fastech, already offer additive manufacturing for the onsite repair of, for example, steam turbine rotors or the rock-wheel trenchers used to grind through concrete.

To restore steel, a thin metal wire is fed into a controlled laser beam, which melts the wire as well as a small region of the existing steel surface. This allows new metal to bond directly to the original metal. By moving the laser across the damaged area, we can build up material only where it is needed. This technique is known as wire-fed laser-directed energy deposition (DED).

This concept builds on weld cladding, used for decades in safety-critical marine and nuclear applications. However, laser-DED enables more localised and controlled addition of new material with a lower heat input.

The electrically powered process makes unusually efficient use of materials. Jason Hutt, director of UK and international business development at Fastech, says the process allows degraded steel to be restored “precisely where material has been lost, potentially extending the life of an asset without replacing the entire structural component”. It could enable shorter interventions and reduce disruption caused by the work.

So why isn’t similar technology used to extend the life of vital UK infrastructure? The key question is how long the repaired structure will remain safe. Bridges are subjected to millions of loading cycles as vehicles pass over them. Even when the stresses are well below those needed to break steel, the repetitive nature of those stresses can open up cracks and then cause them to grow.

This phenomenon, called fatigue, is particularly important in steel bridges, because a repair that looks sound today must remain safe for decades. Independent evidence confirms the genuine potential of wire-fed laser DED for the repair of steel structures. In tests, wire-arc deposition arrested existing fatigue cracks beyond nine million cycles, compared with failure at 0.95 million cycles without repair.

A related but distinct technique called laser cladding also shows promise. Studies to evaluate it show that it restored more than 90% of fatigue strength – the maximum stress steel can withstand over a given number of load cycles – in artificially damaged modern steel.

But much of the scientific evidence comes from small specimens of modern steel that have been artificially damaged. Real bridges may contain century-old steel with different chemical compositions, accumulated fatigue damage and defects from decades of service. Laser deposition also changes the microscopic structure of the steel around the repair.
Engineers need to understand how the old material and the new interact, so that they can assess how much additional safe life the repair provides.

Bridges also provide a tremendous immediate opportunity to mitigate carbon emissions. A recent study found that interventions using UHPFRC, a high-strength construction material, could save 1.7 million tonnes of CO₂ equivalent across just 800 bridges, rising to 7.7 million tonnes across Switzerland’s federal network of 3,903 bridges.

The UK has 16,000 metallic railway bridges alone. When they were surveyed in 2004, 80% were already over 50 years old and half were over 100. The environmental benefits of preserving infrastructure extend beyond the steel itself. Bridge closures can mean weeks or months of diverted journeys, increased congestion and emissions while disrupting public transport, businesses and communities.

Focused renovation can produce 84–93% lower emissions than replacement – even before accounting for indirect emissions from diverted traffic – while reducing the time taken for the intervention and allowing bridges to remain open.

The economic value is equally colossal. The European Commission’s Sustainable Bridges project, set up to increase the use of the European railway network, estimated that a modest 2% increase in residual life across European railway bridge stock could generate savings of the order of €1 billion (£832 million).
And for historic bridges, retaining the original steelwork can protect architectural and cultural heritage that replacement would permanently erase.

We have become accustomed to thinking of technological progress as building something new. As our assets age, extending their safe lives becomes an increasingly important part of the transition to a low-carbon economy.

Offshore wind turbines, industrial facilities and other key structures rely on enormous quantities of steel. Many operate in corrosive environments where replacement is costly and technically challenging. Some of the most important innovations of the coming decades may be those that allow us to preserve what we already have.

articles.title: AI has solved a host of big maths problems – here’s why this threatens the whole field of mathematics
articles.author: Neil Saunders, Senior Lecturer in Mathematics, Department of Mathematical Sciences, City St George's, University of London
paras: For many, the year 2026 will be remembered as the one where mathematics had an identity crisis and forever changed. Frontier (cutting edge) AI models made by OpenAI and Anthropic made stunning progress on hundreds of open problems that have baffled mathematicians for decades – and centuries in some cases.

From April this year, a steady stream of impressive AI-discovered results emerged. It started with a breakthrough by OpenAI on the Erdős unit distance conjecture and the Jacobian conjecture, both of which had been unsolved for decades.

Then, in September and October, two stunning announcements were made. First, Open AI announced a solution to the Navier-Stokes problem – one of the seven “millennium problems” highlighted by the Clay Mathematics Institute in the year 2000. Second, OpenAI released a trove of over 700 papers claiming solutions, proofs or counter-examples (which show that a claim or conjecture is false) to 372 open problems that are at the forefront of mathematics research.

Now, Anthropic researcher Levent Alpöge has announced a Claude-assisted proof of the Riemann Hypothesis. This is arguably the most famous problem in mathematics, proposed by the German mathematician Bernhard Riemann in 1867.

The October “Open AI dump” as it has become known, sent shock waves through the mathematics community because of its sheer scale. Hugo Duminil-Copin, professor and Fields medallist (the medal is a top accolade in mathematics), from the Institute of Advanced Scientific Studies in Paris, said the dump had “annihilated my field of research”. He also warned that it could “dismantle” the discipline of mathematics.

How tech companies were able to make such staggering progress on difficult problems is that first, their specific AI technology, called large language models (LLMs), are trained on the entire human corpus of mathematical literature (and much more).

Second, the companies created “AI-agents”, software systems built around the LLM that extend its capabilities to reasoning, taking actions and executing code. Agents can also observe the results of their actions, taking further action if required.

For the solution to the Navier-Stokes equation, OpenAI set 10,000 AI agents to work collaboratively. It took 88 hours for these agents to find their solution. A further 17 hours was needed to have the solution verified through formalisation and verification software called Lean.

Alpöge’s Claude-assisted proof of the Riemann Hypothesis runs to more than 250,000 pages. The Lean code verification is over 17 million lines long. His Lean proof has since been verified by independent researchers.

Unlike the Poincaré Conjecture, a millennium problem solved by the Russian mathematician Grigori Perelman in the early 2000s, the Navier-Stokes equation, (like all the other 300 problems in the OpenAI dump), was resolved by AI agents with almost no human intervention.

This is truly extraordinary. A metaphor illustrating how these agents work might be a colony of Australian cathedral termites. Each insect in the colony mindlessly does its local thing but in concert, the termites build impressive castles, often over six metres high, replete with ventilation, a form of air conditioning and weather protection.
Likewise, each AI agent chips away at its local task, but collectively, these swarms of agents can now solve – and verify – the hardest known maths problems.
Mass production of results

All this has mathematicians worried. Terence Tao, professor of mathematics at the University of California, Los Angeles and a 2006 Fields medallist, recently suggested that the speed at which mathematical results are being AI-produced is actually harming the discipline.
Tao likened what AI companies are doing as “dumping carcasses of raw meat onto our table and saying ‘here you go, I solved your food problem’.”

On September 11, 2026, Tao and 25 other Fields medallists produced a declaration stating that “the goals of the AI companies and the goals of the mathematical community are severely misaligned”. The declaration warns that “the mass production at faster and faster pace of "true/false” statements could destroy fertile ground instead of breathing life into new ideas".

At the time of writing, this declaration has over 8,000 signatures from mathematicians globally. In a similar spirit, the recently formed Association for Human Mathematics, whose members “commit to conduct entirely AI-free research, centring human thinking and judgement in the mathematical sciences” has more than 1,000 members.

There is an old idiom in AI known as Moravec’s Paradox, which is often expressed as “hard problems are easy and the easy problems are hard”. This phrase explains why we have machines that are better at tasks humans find hard, such as chess, coding and now: mathematical research, but are worse at tasks that humans find easy, such as stacking the dishwasher without breaking plates.

But mathematics is like chess and coding in some sense. It is a somewhat closed world of information that is ripe for AI to come in and extract patterns, find connections and perform calculations that allow it to generate results beyond human capability.

So while fluency and proficiency in “hard” mathematical fields has traditionally been a benchmark of intelligence, both human and machine, these powerful multi-agent AI systems show that raw compute power, combined with an abundance of data, are sufficient to obtain results beyond the reach of many mathematicians over many lifetimes.

However, an interesting footnote to this is that OpenAI estimated that the total cost of finding the solution to the Navier-Stokes equation was US$15 million (£11.4 million) – thus a net loss of US$14 million if the Clay Institute were to award OpenAI the prize money.
Thus, it is possible that the big tech companies will move on from mathematics if they do not see monetary value in continuing to prove open conjectures.

By approaching a problem in a “bottom-up” way, mathematicians build theory and form connections between seemingly disparate sub-disciplines. They disseminate preliminary findings and partial results via journals, conference presentations and workshops.
This engagement with the rest of the community includes PhD students and early career researchers, so that a new generation of mathematicians are being trained to take the field further.

Many students of mathematics go on to fields where a strong mathematical training is invaluable, such as government, data science, education, sustainability, finance and cybersecurity. This ecosystem – essential for a flourishing society and economy – may be at risk if a new “top-down”, black-box, reverse engineered approach to mathematics becomes a new norm.

So while having powerful AI tools to resolve longstanding problems presents new and exciting opportunities – indeed, I believe that there has never been a better time to study maths – these have to be carefully balanced against the wider interests of the discipline as well as the wider interests of society.
Neil Saunders is affiliated with The Campaign for Mathematical Sciences.

articles.title: A new way to extract oxygen from lunar soil could support bases on the Moon
articles.author: Rajani K. Vijayaraghavan, Assistant Professor, Dublin City University
paras: Computer chip manufacturing and lunar exploration seem like completely different worlds. Yet our latest research suggests the two may be more closely connected than expected.
Using technology widely employed in semiconductor manufacturing, we have shown that it is possible to extract oxygen and products containing oxygen from material designed to mimic lunar soil.
This matters because oxygen is one of the most valuable resources for future space exploration. Astronauts need it to breathe, and it is also a major component of rocket propellant.
But transporting large quantities from Earth would be enormously expensive, so space agencies are investigating ways to obtain it directly on the Moon instead.

The challenge is that lunar oxygen does not exist as a readily available gas. Instead, it is chemically bound within minerals that make up the Moon’s surface layer. And although that layer contains a large amount of oxygen by weight, extracting it requires breaking strong chemical bonds within lunar minerals.
Many of the complex techniques that could potentially achieve this extraction would require large amounts of energy.
So our team decided to explore an alternative, lower-temperature approach inspired by a well established industrial technology called “plasma-processing”.

Plasma is often called the fourth state of matter (after solid, liquid and gas). It forms when sufficient energy is supplied to a gas, creating a mixture of charged particles, electrons, and highly reactive chemical species.
In semiconductor fabrication, plasma interacts with silicon dioxide in a process which underpins the production of billions of electronic devices every year.

We asked a simple question: if plasmas are highly effective at reacting with compounds containing oxygen in semiconductor processing, could a similar approach be applied to the oxygen-based compounds in lunar soil?
To investigate, we exposed artificial moon soil (known as lunar regolith simulants) to plasmas generated using gases that are commonly employed in semiconductor manufacturing.
Mining oxygen from moon dust
The results were encouraging. During plasma treatment of the lunar regolith simulants, we detected oxygen and oxygen-containing gaseous products being released.
Further analyses confirmed that the plasma was chemically modifying oxygen-bearing minerals within the material, with some lunar minerals reacting more readily than others.

Understanding these underlying mechanisms is important for enhancing the efficiency of the process and identifying opportunities to improve future systems. But oxygen yields would need to increase substantially before any practical lunar system becomes possible.
Why established technologies matter

One reason this approach is attractive is that it builds on decades of experience developed by the semiconductor industry. Space engineering often requires entirely new technologies, but there are advantages in adapting systems that already exist, are well-understood and have been refined for years on Earth.

The semiconductor industry has spent decades studying how fluorine plasmas interact with materials containing oxygen. Rather than starting from scratch, future researchers can draw on that extensive knowledge base.

There are practical benefits too. Plasma processing is a dry process, avoiding some of the challenges associated with transporting and handling liquid reagents (chemicals added to the process to make a reaction occur) in space. The operating temperatures of plasma processing can also be significantly lower than those required by some conventional oxygen extraction methods.

The implications may extend beyond using oxygen for life support on lunar bases. Lunar soil contains useful elements including silicon, aluminium and iron. While our current work focused on oxygen-bearing reactions, future studies may explore whether plasma-based processes could contribute more broadly to the use of other lunar resources.
Much more research is needed to understand the chemistry, to improve yields and to determine whether the process can be scaled economically.

But the plasma technology that enables the manufacture of billions of transistors may also help humanity tackle one of the biggest challenges of space exploration: learning how to live off the land on another world.

articles.title: Nvidia isn’t the first company to dump a misbehaving CEO – history shows it’s in the interest of corporate boards to act
articles.author: Michael Nalick, Assistant Professor of Management, University of Denver
paras: The story may sound familiar: The CEO of one of the largest and most powerful tech companies resigns over sexual misconduct allegations. The move causes the company’s stock to drop by more than 10%, wiping out billions in value. It also raises scrutiny of the company’s board of directors and whether it made the right decisions ahead of the crisis.
This could easily describe the turmoil facing Nvidia after the ouster of its CEO, Jensen Huang. But it actually transpired over 15 years ago at Hewlett Packard, under CEO Mark Hurd.

Jensen Huang is just the latest in a long line of CEOs who lost their jobs over personal misconduct. And as with HP, scrutiny is shifting from his behavior to his board – and the decisions that led to his exit.

Prominent industry leaders are questioning the board’s decision to oust him. They include Peter Steinberger of OpenAI, Anduril Industries co-founder Palmer Luckey, Elon Musk, Replit CEO Amjad Masad, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan. Meanwhile, an internal petition allegedly signed by more than 1,600 Nvidia employees has also called for Jensen Huang’s reinstatement.

As a scholar of management who has researched corporate misconduct, I believe the board made the right call. After collecting instances of CEO personal misconduct dating back to 1995, I have repeatedly found that doing nothing, as a board, is worse than doing something.

CEO personal misconduct isn’t simply a private matter or an isolated leadership failure. I believe it creates reputational and governance risks for directors and can embolden further misconduct when left unaddressed. It may also signal deeper problems within the organization.
But it’s still hard for boards to act, particularly when the CEO is also the company’s founder and a central figure in its success. If the board is earning billions, it’s even more difficult.

One important change over the years is that boards are becoming more sensitive to misconduct matters due to greater scrutiny by the media and public. They’re also more aware of the consequences for their own job that stem from the board’s performance and entanglement in the misconduct. In fact, directors of companies whose CEOs are involved in personal misconduct exit at a significantly higher rate than normal, either because they choose to leave a messy situation or because they’re forced out due to poor performance, my research shows.

One of the better known examples is Best Buy founder Richard Schulze, who stepped down as chairman of the board in 2012 after an internal investigation revealed that he knew about former CEO Brian Dunn’s inappropriate personal relationship with a female employee and failed to report it.

Directors are also personally penalized for their association with their company’s corporate misconduct. They may lose their board seats or see other companies they’re associated with take a hit. And if they hold executive positions elsewhere, the misconduct may spill over to damage the reputations of those companies as well.
In other words, directors have a rational basis to be concerned about their reputations and how a CEO’s personal misconduct may tarnish it.

In the case of Nvidia, questions are now being asked about the rigor of board oversight, the lack of CEO succession planning, and whether the board knew anything about the affairs. These questions have now spread to issues of potential national security risks.

Another issue is moral hazard: when someone acts recklessly because they know someone else will bear the cost if things go wrong. Assuming individual directors do face penalties for CEO personal misconduct, they have to address the likelihood of incentivizing further misconduct if the CEO is retained, which would further stain their reputation.
My research has found that risk to be high.

When CEOs are caught engaging in misconduct and the board doesn’t act, it can create a moral-hazard precedent and emboldens the CEO to behave badly again. In fact, when CEOs engage in repeated personal misconduct, the second instance is often even worse than the first.

Take former American Airlines CEO Doug Parker, who was the subject of two publicly reported DUI arrests. The second incident, in 2007, attracted considerably more media attention while prompting criticism of the board for allegedly failing to disclose the first incident in 1991.

Christopher Kubasik is another example of a second chance gone wrong. He was recently ousted as CEO of defense contractor L3Harris Technologies, more than 14 years after being forced out of Lockheed Martin following allegations of similar personal misconduct involving an inappropriate relationship.

In the case of Nvidia, Jensen reportedly lied to company officials about the nature of his intimate relationships for more than a year. From the board’s perspective, if he lied about this, what else has he lied about? And if they let him off the hook, what would he lie about in the future?
Broader, often uncomfortable questions about company culture are also at stake.

CEO personal misconduct can be a symptom of a larger cultural problem at the company, my research shows. And it’s often associated with other types of corporate misconduct that affect the very operations of a business. In fact, other types of corporate misconduct frequently occur around a similar time frame as the personal misconduct of an executive.

Take Dov Charney’s tenure as CEO of American Apparel. During his leadership, the company faced significant accounting problems in 2009-10 that required it to re-audit several years of financial statements. Around the same time, Charney faced multiple allegations of personal misconduct, including sexual harassment, sexual assault, racist remarks and abusive behavior toward employees.

It’s in boards’ interest to grasp that personal misconduct can indicate a larger organizational issue – and, as a result, lead to more scrutiny of the board. With Nvidia, for example, there’s now a spotlight on the company’s organizational culture, its financial dealings and its possible role in skirting U.S. sanctions on Chinese chip import restrictions. The board is likely looking at the totality of the issues and not just the personal misconduct.

For now, the public debate has largely centered on what the company might lose without Jensen Huang at the helm. An equally important question, though, is what the company and its board might risk by retaining a CEO whose conduct has raised serious questions about judgment, trust and organizational oversight.

It’s a board’s duty to protect its organization from managers who go astray, as legendary investor Warren Buffett noted: “It isn’t fundamental dishonesty that causes people to go in a different direction. It’s human nature. There are plenty of people who are really decent people, intelligent people. … But they just don’t come to grips with reality. And boards usually don’t push them to.”

articles.title: The US-China AI race is real – but Trump’s recent moves on ‘super intelligence’ are unlikely to give America any advantage
articles.author: Ram Gopal, Professor of Information Systems Management, Warwick Business School, University of Warwick
paras: Donald Trump is insisting that people drop their use of the term artificial intelligence (AI), in favour of “super intelligence”. This started on September 29, when he signed an executive order telling federal agencies to call AI super intelligence, because, in the president’s view, “artificial” makes it sound fake.
On October 4, he followed up with a super intelligence force to coordinate the federal government’s effort “to ensure that America continues to lead the world in Super Intelligence”.

This AI force is led by Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence and a former chair of the Securities and Exchange Commission. Alongside him sit Federal Trade Commission chair Andrew Ferguson, the Pentagon’s technology chief Emil Michael and Scott Kupor, who runs the federal workforce.
The force reports to the president and his chief of staff and has 120 days to report on the risks and opportunities AI poses.

Is this serious national strategy or a branding exercise? The label itself tells us very little. What matters is whether the force can marshal what actually decides who leads in AI: compute, capital, talent and infrastructure. This is now a race, and the countries and organisations that move fastest and mobilise the most resources will hold a significant advantage.

Supporters can point to a genuine coordination problem. Responsibility for AI in Washington is scattered across intelligence, defence, competition policy, procurement and the civil service, which rarely act in concert.
Putting several of those agencies under one roof, reporting directly to the White House, could cut through that. Clayton has given a blunt assessment: “The risk of not being first is high.”

America also has a strong hand. According to Stanford’s 2026 AI Index, US private investment in AI reached US$285.9 billion (£217.24 billion) in 2025, roughly 23 times China’s US$12.4 billion (£9.42 billion). America’s largest tech firms are on track to spend more than US$650 billion on capital investment this year.

A body that helps clear bottlenecks the private sector cannot – grid connections, data centre permitting (approval), hiring technical talent into government – could add real value. Including the head of the federal workforce is a telling choice: governments have long struggled to recruit the people they need for AI.

Critics see something much thinner. The White House has not disclosed a budget, nor said whether the force will have regulatory powers or merely advise. It arrived shortly after leading firms, including OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta and Nvidia, had signed a one-page White House accord committing to internal evaluations, external audits and board reviews.

Trump called it “morally binding”. But Democrat lawmaker Mark Warner, senior senator from Virginia, was scathing: “The president’s response? To rename it and tell the companies developing it to regulate themselves,” he said.

To my mind, there are three deeper problems. First, the US does not control the trajectory of AI. The same Stanford report found that the performance gap between the best US and Chinese models has narrowed to 2.7%, down from double digits in 2023.

Beijing will pursue its own strategy whatever Washington calls its task force. Second, the actors that matter most are private. The frontier AI labs (those at the cutting edge) have enormous commercial and strategic incentives of their own – and the previously mentioned investment figures are overwhelmingly made up of private money.

The companies will cooperate where interests align, on energy or export controls, for example. But I would not expect them to commit fully to a government programme. A voluntary accord with no enforcement mechanism shows where the leverage lies.

The third problem is timing. The US midterm elections heavily shifted control of Congress in the Democrats’ favour. This could reshape both funding for AI and oversight. Building national AI capability is a multi-year effort, and what is created by executive action can be undone the same way. For instance, President Trump revoked Joe Biden’s AI executive order on his first day back in office.

There is also a tension in the mandate itself. The force is asked both to win a race and to protect the public, yet its leadership is drawn from the intelligence, defence and competition enforcement sectors rather than from AI safety. Those goals do not always point the same way, and the announcement about the super intelligence force says little about how they will be balanced.

Is this better than nothing? Absolutely. Coordination has value, and the force could become a serious mechanism for concentrating resources at a scale commensurate with the stakes. But the test is not the name. It is whether the body secures a substantial budget, gains real authority over approval for infrastructure, procurement and hiring, and survives the political cycle.

AI policy is at a turning point. Yet a name, like super intelligence, is just a slogan. Until we see what resources the super intelligence force can command, and whether it can execute quickly and sustain that effort, I would put relatively little faith in it changing the trajectory of AI.

articles.title: Why AI-enabled scientific research is a double-edged sword
articles.author: James A. R. Marshall, Director, Centre for Machine Intelligence, University of Sheffield
paras: OpenAI has sparked a backlash in the mathematics community by apparently using AI to solve more than 700 longstanding maths problems in a short space of time. A recent open letter signed by 28 recipients of the Fields Medal (one of the highest honours in maths) goes some way to explaining why.

Mathematicians who have gone through some of the solutions offered by AI say they are opaque in their reasoning. As the open letter explains: “Solving problems is only a tool and proxy for achieving the primary goal of conceptual understanding and insight.”

As famed mathematician and Fields Medal winner Terence Tao put it: “These companies are dumping carcasses of raw meat onto our communal village table and saying: ‘Here you go, I solved your food problem.‘”
OpenAI said it had consulted with the community prior to announcing the latest three results, one of which was in my own field of computer science.

Nevertheless, mathematicians are having to adapt fast to the disruptive arrival of AI in their field. This challenge extends far beyond mathematics and into all other disciplines of science and research.
The impact AI has had on software development through tools such as Claude and Codex, is undeniable. Industry software teams are now routinely using AI tools in their work.

But now, AI is already having a major impact on the practice of science itself. Academic journals and conferences are dealing with exponential increases in submissions from researchers, in a system largely based on volunteer effort for reviewing and editing.

This year, the International Conference on Learning Representations, a leading academic meeting on AI, received 60,000 submissions. This has increased from 490 in 2017. One researcher, commenting on the figures, said: “AI is breaking traditional academic peer review.”

This doesn’t seem to be a special case. In 2024, Mark A Hanson, from the University of Exeter, and colleagues, published a paper titled: “The strain on scientific publishing”. In it, the authors note that the total number of available academic articles has grown exponentially in recent years.

This is in part the result of a decades-long trend, predating modern generative AI, with many factors playing a role – including pressure on researchers to publish large numbers of academic articles, known as “publish or perish”. In 2022, just before ChatGPT launched, the number of papers published was about 47% higher than in 2016. The increase has occurred while the number of practising scientists has seen little growth. But AI is undoubtedly accelerating the process.

Yet this raises questions about whether the current trajectory is sustainable – and whether the quality of science will suffer. One academic conference has been testing whether AI could be part of the solution as well as the problem. This year, the NeurIPS meeting, which focuses on AI and machine learning, introduced a voluntary AI-assisted review for those submitting conference abstracts.
Afterwards, scientists evaluated the quality of the review and how helpful it was. But some in the field believe this could compound current problems.
Protecting critical thinking

Anecdotal evidence suggests some members of the public who are not professional scientists are using AI to produce and submit their own academic papers and write books on science. Citizen scientists make valuable contributions in areas such as biodiversity monitoring and astronomy.

But AI should not be viewed as a substitute for the formal training, daily research work, critical thinking and expert input from colleagues that academia offers. While AI and related technologies are powerful tools for democratising knowledge, it took me 13 years from my PhD to write my first book (the only one I have written so far), whereas now the same can apparently be done in weeks. But, as with peer review and maths proofs, humans have to check and interpret these.
As this story plays through and repeats, we may need to resort to new modes of scientific dissemination to deal with the new methods of creating research.

This brings me to the critical thinking that research requires. Currently, I provide the ideas, but increasingly rely on my AI assistant to do a lot of the work of thinking for me, or at least appear to. But the results of AI-enabled research can be obtuse, as the Terence Tao quote above illustrates, or even plain wrong. They can only be sorted out with human time and domain expertise.

I increasingly wonder what this means for the role of the researcher and for training the future generation of scientists, mathematicians and engineers. I am finding that a challenging, long term student project that would normally take several months to complete is at risk of being able to be almost completely automated through providing judicious prompts to an AI agent.

If I am guiding the student while they provide the prompts to an AI system, what do they learn from the process? And in my own research, where AI enables me to undertake projects I would not otherwise have the resources to, if I am providing the ideas but the AI is doing a lot of the “thinking” for me, am I even doing my own research anymore?
This could have an impact on the future generation’s ability to generate novel research questions, as well as their capacity for critiquing AI’s attempts to answer them.

One of my favourite sci-fi short stories is Profession, by Isaac Asimov. In it, the author imagines a future where young adults are educated by direct upload into their brains using technology known as magnetic tapes – which could be seen as a stand-in for AI. At one point, the main protagonist, George, tries to convince another character that humans can learn in other ways – by reading books, for example.

The other person is baffled, seeing this only as an unnecessary expense. Through the narrative, Asimov reveals the risks in the “direct upload” approach to learning. He also explores what is needed for society to progress when some forms of knowledge can be gained so easily.

We seem to be arriving at the science fiction future I once looked forward to where, like a science officer on a starship exploring unknown corners of the universe, or a billionaire genius tech superhero, I can just provide the ideas while getting the computer to do the heavy lifting. Like others, I am exhilarated by this, but also concerned about what it means for the practice and future of my discipline.

articles.title: AI helps uncover critical flaw in ubiquitous internet software
articles.author: Doug Jacobson, University Professor of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Iowa State University
paras: If you checked your bank balance, booked a flight or ordered groceries online today, there is a good chance your request was handled by a computer program written in Java.

For nearly three decades, the Java programming language has been one of the quiet workhorses of the internet. While most people rarely interact with it directly on their phones or laptops, it sits at the heart of most large, behind-the-scenes server applications that power modern business, finance and government.

That ubiquity is why a new critical security alert from the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency drew the attention of technology teams worldwide. Security researchers uncovered a severe flaw, dubbed Java4Shell, in a core Java component. If left unpatched, the bug could allow an attacker to trick a vulnerable server into executing malicious code.

As a cybersecurity researcher who studies how large-scale software systems fail and how to defend them, I see this discovery as both a standard call to action for system administrators and another milestone in a broader shift: Artificial intelligence is rapidly changing how hidden flaws in critical software are discovered.
To understand the vulnerability, it helps to know why Java became so popular in the first place.

Normally, software must be tailored to the specific computer hardware and operating system it runs on. Java solved that headache with a clever piece of software called the Java Virtual Machine. It is essentially a program that runs other programs. Software developers write their Java application once, and the Java Virtual Machine provides a uniform foundation on top of a server’s operating system, running that application regardless of the underlying machine.

In addition to running the application, the Java Virtual Machine provides a standardized set of code for everyday tasks, such as reading files, managing network connections and formatting incoming data.

One of those routine tasks is Base64 encoding. Computers often need to send complex data, such as images, attachments or authentication tokens, over text-based internet protocols. Because raw binary data can be corrupted in transit, systems convert it into a string of standard text characters using Base64. When a Java server receives that string, its Base64 library decodes it back into its original form so the application can use it.
Inside the flaw and why AI matters

The newly discovered vulnerability resides in the Base64 decoding library in Oracle’s implementation of the Java Virtual Machine. This means that any application using this version of the Java Virtual Machine is at risk.

According to technical analysis of the flaw, a carefully crafted piece of malformed Base64 data can overwhelm the library’s processing, allowing an attacker to break out of normal boundaries, execute unauthorized commands and potentially gain control of the server.

If this sounds familiar, it follows a pattern seen recently with a high-profile PHP vulnerability, another foundational web language. Like the PHP vulnerability, this Java flaw was uncovered by cybersecurity firm Calif using AI tools to search for vulnerabilities.

Calif officials said the company alerted the governments of the United States, Canada, Australia, New Zealand and Britain, and major tech companies, including Google and Microsoft, before the Java vulnerability became public. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency then issued its alert, urging organizations to immediately patch the flaw.

Historically, identifying subtle memory or parsing errors buried deep within millions of lines of mature code required months of painstaking manual review by human experts. Today, security researchers are pairing AI tools with traditional code analysis to systematically probe software libraries for edge cases that humans might overlook for years.
Whenever a critical vulnerability affects a foundational piece of software, headlines can sound alarmist. In reality, there are several reasons to maintain perspective while still acting quickly.

First, the good news is that a responsible security researcher discovered and privately reported this flaw, giving people who maintain software time to develop and release a fix before attackers could widely exploit it.
Second, everyday users do not need to panic about their personal devices. This is an issue affecting enterprise applications and cloud infrastructure, not home laptops, smartphones or tablets.

Third, even on vulnerable servers, exploiting this bug in the real world is not always straightforward. Most modern web systems do not expose raw Java decoders directly to the open internet. Instead, incoming traffic typically passes through several types of software – firewalls, load balancers and web proxies – that inspect, sanitize or reject malformed data before it reaches the underlying Java application.

Still, “harder to exploit” does not mean impossible, especially for internal systems or custom applications that pass user-supplied bits of information, called tokens, directly to Java’s decoder. As with any foundational infrastructure repair, the best defense is straightforward: promptly applying the latest security updates.
As AI accelerates the discovery of long-hidden software flaws, keeping the digital infrastructure patched remains one of the most effective cybersecurity practices.
